resources.string: DNS protection · No ads · No tracking
DNS protection through a local VPN

Android uses a local VPN so DNSBunker can send system DNS queries to dnsbunker.org over encrypted connections. Other internet traffic connects directly. Apps using their own DNS may bypass this protection. Another VPN will be disconnected. The app sends no telemetry.
Standard mode protects system DNS. Enable public port-53 interception under Wi-Fi for broader coverage. Apps using their own encrypted DNS can bypass either mode.
Protection stays on for unknown Wi-Fi networks. Only networks you explicitly add are exempt.
On exempt Wi-Fi, the network handles DNS. The app cannot verify its encryption. Wi-Fi names can be impersonated.
Connections to devices on your local network remain direct. The app routes only DNS traffic to its virtual DNS addresses.
Local names are always kept away from the public resolver. This switch permits local resolution only with the additional permissions below.
Resolve local names through the private DNS server only on explicitly trusted Wi-Fi.
Trust this Wi-Fi for local names
Without consent, local lookups fail safely. Optional router DNS uses unencrypted UDP on the local network. Public DNSBunker connections remain encrypted.
The DNSBunker tunnel will stop on this Wi-Fi. The network will handle DNS; the app cannot verify its encryption. Wi-Fi names can be impersonated.
Names such as nas.home.arpa are sent to the private DNS server only on trusted Wi-Fi. These local queries are unencrypted and visible on the network. Public queries to DNSBunker remain encrypted.
A block requires an explicit DNSBunker RPZ marker (PRO/TIF) or EDE 15. NXDOMAIN alone is not a block. App health probes are excluded.
EDNS padding rounds query sizes to 128-byte blocks. It does not hide domain names.
Check DNS resolution periodically and attempt recovery after connection failures.
If DoH fails, try DNSBunker over certificate-verified TLS on port 853. No public plaintext fallback.
This app connects to DNSBunker using DoH/2, HTTP/3, DoT or DoQ with certificate verification. If encrypted resolution fails, it does not silently switch to public plaintext DNS.
No ads, no trackers, no account. Settings stay on your device. DNS queries are sent encrypted to dnsbunker.org for resolution.

DNS queries, not people or attacks. PRO and TIF are resolver filter zones; they do not prove a prevented attack.
Your actual measurements appear here once the app answers DNS queries.

HTTP/3 and DoQ use QUIC. If UDP is blocked, HTTPS over TCP/443 remains an option. Direct IP connections without hostname SNI help with some SNI blocks. They cannot bypass blocked server IPs or a pending Wi-Fi login.
Open Android Wi-Fi sign-in. DNSBunker does not automatically disable protection. The network and Android handle the sign-in itself.

DNSBunker receives the DNS question and sees your public source IP to resolve it. The connection is encrypted. The linked official policy covers service-side processing. This app stores no domain names and sends no telemetry. Settings stay local; counters and the 2-hour chart stay only in memory until process exit or reset. Wi-Fi names are stored only for rules you explicitly set. Android backups are disabled. Optional router DNS is separately permitted, unencrypted local UDP.
Counters and the chart in this app will reset. No domain names are stored.
Since app start · only on this device
Your DNS queries are encrypted and sent to DNSBunker.

Redirects public UDP/TCP port-53 queries to DNSBunker. The local IP tunnel also handles ordinary TCP/UDP traffic for this. Local networks remain directly reachable. Other apps’ own DoH/DoT can still bypass DNS filtering.
The IP stack is unavailable on this device. Comprehensive interception cannot be enabled.

In comprehensive mode, other packets also stay on-device: the app connects directly to the original destination and keeps no connection logs. Other apps’ TLS remains unchanged; there is no remote VPN exit.
A battery-optimization exemption can reduce background disconnections. Android or the device vendor may still stop the app. Continuous operation can use more battery.
Private DNS can bypass this local DNS protection and cause warnings or incomplete statistics. It should be off during normal app use. The app does not change this system setting itself.

Classification uses the RPZ/CNAME marker reported by the resolver. PRO covers ads, tracking, telemetry and other content. TIF denotes threat lists. A blocked query does not prove that an attack was prevented.
Warm DNS timings exclude initial connection setup. Total wait includes handshake, queueing, retries and fallback. These are network timings, not pure server processing time.

Wi-Fi exceptions need the location permission and location turned on. Otherwise Android hides the network name.
Exceptions are paused while Android’s “Block connections without VPN” is on.
Protection restarts automatically after updates and restarts. For even more reliability, select DNSBunker as always-on VPN in Android.
Another VPN or Android ended DNSBunker. Tap to turn protection back on.
Exceptions apply right after a restart only if Android allows location access “all the time”. Otherwise they start working once you open the app.
